Metadata was rediscovered during fallback decisions. That made it possible for malformed or unreadable metadata to be interpreted as “this feature is not present,” after which `git.PlainOpen` might be attempted.

Now the shape is:

```text
OpenPath(root)
    |
    v
ResolveWorktreeMetadata(root)
    |
    +-- metadata absent ------------> validate and open as bare repo
    |
    +-- metadata malformed/error ---> stop; do not fall back
    |
    +-- valid metadata
           |
           v
       WorktreeMetadata
       ├── GitDir
       ├── CommonDir
       └── WorktreeID
           |
           v
       openWorktreeRepository(root, metadata)
           ├── detect alternates from metadata
           └── inspect reftable from metadata
```

The important architectural change is:

> Resolve physical Git metadata once, then pass the resulting facts down. Do not let lower-level operations rediscover them.

## The functions that changed

| Before | Now | Architectural effect |
|---|---|---|
| `openPathWithAlternates(root)` | `openWorktreeRepository(root, metadata)` | Repository opening consumes already-resolved metadata instead of resolving it internally. |
| `repoUsesReftable(...) bool` | `inspectRepoUsesReftable(...) (bool, error)` | “Could not inspect” is no longer silently treated as “does not use reftable.” |
| `hasObjectAlternates(root)` | `hasObjectAlternates(metadata)` | Alternates detection no longer traverses `.git` and `commondir` again. |
| Scattered resolution during `OpenPath` | `ResolveWorktreeMetadata(root)` | One canonical resolution pass returns all three metadata facts. |

The main new public API is in [metadata.go](/Users/muskanpaliwal/Work/open-source/entire/cli/refactor-git-metadata-owner/cmd/entire/cli/gitrepo/metadata.go):

```go
type WorktreeMetadata struct {
    GitDir    string
    CommonDir string
    WorktreeID string
}

func ResolveWorktreeMetadata(explicitRoot string) (WorktreeMetadata, error)
```

Internally, the resolver now owns operations such as:

- Resolving whether `.git` is a directory or a Git worktree pointer file.
- Reading and validating `commondir`.
- Computing the linked-worktree ID.
- Ensuring resolved metadata paths are real directories.
- Handling symlinks and `..` without changing path meaning during lexical cleaning.
- Distinguishing “no worktree metadata exists” from “metadata exists but is broken.”

The repository-opening policy lives in [repository.go](/Users/muskanpaliwal/Work/open-source/entire/cli/refactor-git-metadata-owner/cmd/entire/cli/gitrepo/repository.go).

Today, the only production entry point directly calling `ResolveWorktreeMetadata` is `gitrepo.OpenPath`.

Inside that path:

- `OpenPath` asks for canonical metadata.
- `openWorktreeRepository` uses `GitDir` and `CommonDir`.
- Alternates detection consumes that metadata.
- Reftable inspection consumes that metadata.
- Bare-repository handling happens only when the resolver positively reports that worktree metadata is absent.
- `git.PlainOpen` remains available, but only after valid worktree metadata has been established and specialized features are positively absent.

`WorktreeID` is already calculated and validated, but `OpenPath` does not have much use for it itself. It mainly prepares the canonical result for the later checkpoint/session migrations.

## What was deliberately not removed?

This is the most important scope boundary: GMT-001 did not delete the legacy ecosystem.

These still exist:

- `resolveDotGitPath`
- `resolveCommonGitPath`
- `paths.GetWorktreeID`
- Direct `git rev-parse --git-common-dir` calls
- Consumer-specific `.git` traversal in checkpoint, session, strategy, settings, trail, and agent integrations

The formerly exported `ResolveDotGitPath` and `ResolveCommonGitPath` are now private, but remain temporarily because Codex hook discovery still uses them.

So the current codebase temporarily has two worlds:

```text
New canonical world
└── gitrepo.OpenPath
    └── ResolveWorktreeMetadata

Legacy world
├── checkpoint
├── session
├── strategy and hooks
├── settings
├── trail
└── some agent integrations
    ├── paths.GetWorktreeID
    ├── old gitrepo helpers
    └── git rev-parse --git-common-dir
```

The ownership guard test records the remaining legacy sites. It acts as a migration fence: existing exceptions are temporarily allowed, but adding new independent metadata traversal should fail the guard.

## The new responsibility boundaries

There are now three distinct layers:

| Layer | Responsibility |
|---|---|
| `paths.WorktreeRoot` | Discover which worktree the command is operating in. This may depend on CWD or command context. |
| `gitrepo.ResolveWorktreeMetadata` | Interpret the physical Git metadata layout for an explicit worktree root. |
| `gitdir` | Safely read and write inside a Git directory that has already been selected. |

That distinction matters because resolution, policy, and file access are different jobs.

For example, suppose a checkpoint operation needs the common Git directory:

```text
Bad future shape:
checkpoint independently reads .git and commondir

Intended future shape:
checkpoint
    └── ResolveWorktreeMetadata(root)
        └── metadata.CommonDir
```

But checkpoint still owns its product policy:

- Whether missing metadata is fatal.
- What user-facing error to print.
- Which checkpoint files to read.
- Whether an operation is allowed for a bare repository.

The resolver provides facts; it does not make every caller’s policy decisions.

## Concrete layouts

For a normal checkout:

```text
/repo/.git/
```

The result is approximately:

```go
WorktreeMetadata{
    GitDir:     "/repo/.git",
    CommonDir:  "/repo/.git",
    WorktreeID: "",
}
```

For a linked worktree:

```text
/main/.git/                         common Git directory
/main/.git/worktrees/feature/       per-worktree Git directory
/feature/.git                       pointer to the per-worktree directory
```

The result is approximately:

```go
WorktreeMetadata{
    GitDir:     "/main/.git/worktrees/feature",
    CommonDir:  "/main/.git",
    WorktreeID: "feature",
}
```

Previously, different consumers could derive different portions of this relationship using slightly different logic. The eventual goal is for every consumer to receive the same coherent three-part answer.

## Where the remaining GMT slices fit

The checkpoint-backed plan is:

1. GMT-001 — establish `WorktreeMetadata`, the canonical resolver, and repository-opening integration.
2. GMT-002 — migrate checkpoint consumers.
3. GMT-003 — migrate session consumers.
4. GMT-004 — migrate strategy and hook consumers.
5. GMT-005 — migrate remaining callers and delete the legacy resolution functions.

So the current state is intentionally transitional:

> GMT-001 built and validated the destination. GMT-002 through GMT-005 move the callers. GMT-005 earns the large deletion.
